blocks.text: Every MCP server talks to something beyond itself, a database, a payment provider, a calendar API, a search index. Reaching any of those requires a credential, and that credential is a secret the server must hold onto but never expose.

Secrets management is the practice of storing, loading, and rotating those credentials without ever letting them leak into source code, logs, or the wrong hands. It sounds simple, yet it is one of the most common ways real servers get compromised.
This lesson covers what secrets an MCP server typically holds, why hardcoding them is dangerous, and how to load and rotate them safely.
1. What Counts as a Secret
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441161921-608923604.png

A secret is any piece of information that grants access, and that would cause harm if someone else obtained it. For an MCP server this usually means credentials that let it act on behalf of a user or a company against some other system.

The three most common categories are API keys for upstream services, database credentials, and OAuth client secrets. Each of these shows up in almost every non trivial MCP deployment, so each deserves its own close look.
A simple test helps decide whether something counts as a secret, ask whether you would be comfortable pasting it into a public chat channel. If the answer is no, treat it as a secret.
2. API Keys for Upstream Services

Most MCP servers exist to connect a client to some other service, a weather API, a payments platform, an internal analytics tool. Reaching that service almost always requires an API key issued by the provider.

That key is often long lived and broadly scoped by default, which makes it especially attractive to an attacker. Whoever holds it can usually call the upstream service exactly as the legitimate server would.

blocks.title: A quiet risk
blocks.content: An upstream API key leaking is often worse than a leak of the MCP server's own credentials, because the upstream provider has no idea the request is not coming from you.

blocks.text: Many providers let you issue several keys at once, each scoped to a smaller set of permissions. Using a narrow key for each purpose limits what a single leak can reach.
3. Database Credentials

An MCP server that reads or writes persistent data needs a database username and password, or a connection string that bundles both together. This credential is the single gate protecting everything stored behind it.

Database credentials are especially dangerous to leak because a database rarely limits what a valid credential can see. A single leaked connection string can expose every table the server was ever allowed to touch.
Where possible, create a database user scoped only to what the MCP server needs, rather than reusing an administrator account out of convenience.
4. OAuth Client Secrets

When an MCP server acts on a user's behalf against a third party using OAuth, it registers as a client application and receives a client secret alongside its client id. That secret proves to the authorization server that token requests are really coming from your server.

Unlike a user's own access token, the client secret does not belong to any single user. It belongs to the server itself, so a leak of it can be used to impersonate the server across every user who has ever connected through it.
This is one reason OAuth client secrets deserve at least as much care as the individual access tokens they help produce, covered separately in the OAuth lesson.
5. Why Hardcoding Secrets Fails
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441161921-88989320.png
Hardcoding means writing the literal secret value directly inside a source file, right next to the code that uses it. It feels convenient in the moment, and it is almost always a mistake.

Once a secret is typed into a file, it becomes part of that file's history the moment it is committed. Deleting it in a later commit does not remove it, the old value still sits in every earlier commit anyone can check out.

items: A hardcoded secret gets copied every time someone clones or forks the repository
It gets shared automatically with every collaborator who has read access to the code
It shows up in code review tools, CI logs, and editor history without anyone intending it to
Rotating it means finding and editing every file that contains it, then redeploying

blocks.text: 6. Environment Variables as the Baseline
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441161922-314620479.png

The simplest fix is to keep the secret out of the file entirely and read it from an environment variable at runtime instead. The value lives in the process environment, set by whoever deploys the server, not in anything that gets committed.
This one change already solves the biggest problem with hardcoding, the secret no longer travels with the source code. Anyone who can read the repository still cannot read the credential.
Environment variables are also the same mechanism most hosting platforms already use for configuration, so adopting them adds no new infrastructure.
7. Loading a Secret the Right Way
Compare a hardcoded key against one read from the environment. The difference in the code itself is small, but the difference in what a leaked repository exposes is enormous.

code.content:
# Never do this. The literal key now lives in git history forever.
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY = "<STRIPE_SECRET_KEY>"

# Do this instead. The value is supplied by the environment, never written down.
import os
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY = os.environ["STRIPE_SECRET_KEY"]
if not STRIPE_SECRET_KEY:
    raise RuntimeError("STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is not set")

blocks.text: Notice the second version also fails loudly if the variable is missing, rather than silently running with an empty key. A missing secret should stop startup, not produce a confusing error later.
7.1 Failing Loudly on a Missing Secret
A server that starts successfully without a required secret often fails much later, deep inside a confusing stack trace when it finally tries to use the missing value.
Checking for every required secret at startup, and refusing to start without it, turns that confusing later failure into a clear, immediate one.
8. Beyond Environment Variables, Dedicated Secret Stores

blocks.alt: Beyond Environment Variables, Dedicated Secret Stores
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441161922-217989259.png

Environment variables are a fine starting point, but they have limits at real scale. They are usually visible to anything running in the same process or container, they do not rotate themselves, and they leave no audit trail of who read what.

A dedicated secret store, such as a cloud provider's secrets manager or a tool built specifically for this, solves those gaps. Secrets are encrypted at rest, access is logged, and rotation can be automated centrally instead of by hand.
9. Comparing Environment Variables and Secret Managers
Neither approach is universally correct. The right choice depends on how many secrets a server holds and how often they need to change.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Best fit","Rotation story"],"rows":[["Environment variables","Small servers, few secrets, simple deployments","Manual, requires a restart to pick up a new value"],["Dedicated secret store","Larger deployments, many secrets, compliance needs","Can be automated, often without a restart"],["Hardcoded in source","Never a good fit","Effectively impossible without a full audit of history"]]}

blocks.text: It is common to start with environment variables and move to a dedicated secret store as a server grows, and there is nothing wrong with that progression.
10. Keeping Secrets Out of Version Control Files

Local development often uses a file, commonly named something like a dotenv file, to hold environment variables for convenience. That file must never be committed, or it becomes exactly the hardcoding problem it was meant to avoid.

Add the file to the project's ignore list from the very first commit, not after a secret has already slipped in. Provide a template file with placeholder values instead, so new contributors know what variables they need without ever seeing a real one.
If a real secret does slip into a commit, changing the ignore list afterward is not enough, the value already exists in history and must be treated as leaked and rotated.
11. Secrets Leaking Through Logs and Errors

blocks.alt: Secrets Leaking Through Logs and Errors
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441161923-382472161.png
A secret does not only leak through source code. A poorly written error message or a debug log line that prints request headers or connection strings can expose the same value just as permanently.

blocks.title: Check what you log
blocks.content: Before logging a request, a config object, or an error, ask whether any field in it could be a credential. If in doubt, redact it rather than print it.

blocks.text: Error tracking tools that capture full stack traces and request bodies are a frequent, easy to overlook source of this same leak.
12. Least Privilege for Every Secret
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441162162-958046989.png
A secret should carry only the access it actually needs, nothing broader. A database credential used only for reading customer support tickets should not also be able to drop tables.

Scoping secrets tightly does not prevent a leak, but it limits the damage a leaked one can do. This is the same principle covered in the Access Control lesson, applied to credentials instead of user permissions.
It is worth revisiting each secret's scope periodically, since permissions tend to grow wider over time as new features borrow an existing credential instead of requesting a narrower one.
13. Designing for Rotation From Day One

blocks.alt: Designing for Rotation From Day One
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441162164-324993942.png

Rotation means replacing an old secret value with a new one on a schedule, or immediately after a suspected leak. A server designed with rotation in mind treats the secret as something that changes, not as a fixed constant.

The practical requirement is simple, the server must fetch the current secret value rather than baking one value in for its entire lifetime. Everything else in a rotation friendly design follows from that one habit.
Teams that only think about rotation after a leak often discover their server has no way to pick up a new value without a full redeploy, which turns an urgent fix into a slow one.
14. A Rotation Friendly Pattern

One reliable pattern is to cache a secret briefly in memory, then refresh it on a timer instead of only reading it once at startup. That way a rotated secret takes effect within minutes instead of requiring a full redeploy.

code.content:
import time

_cached_key = None
_cached_at = 0
CACHE_SECONDS = 300

def get_api_key():
    global _cached_key, _cached_at
    now = time.time()
    if _cached_key is None or now - _cached_at > CACHE_SECONDS:
        _cached_key = fetch_secret("stripe_api_key")
        _cached_at = now
    return _cached_key

blocks.text: Because the function always checks the cache age before using a value, a rotated secret in the store is picked up automatically the next time the cache expires. No one has to remember to restart the server.
15. Rotating a Secret Without Breaking a Running Server

The trick to rotating safely is overlap, keeping the old value valid for a short window while the new one is introduced. That way in flight requests using the old credential still succeed while new requests move over to the new one.

items: Generate the new secret alongside the old one, without disabling the old one yet
Update the secret store or environment so the server can fetch the new value
Let the server pick up the new value naturally, either on its next cache refresh or its next restart
Confirm the server is successfully using the new value by checking logs or a health check
Disable the old secret only once nothing is still using it

blocks.title: Never rotate by deleting first
blocks.content: Disabling the old secret before the new one is confirmed working is how a routine rotation turns into an outage.

blocks.text: Providers that support only a single active key at a time make this overlap harder, so it is worth checking that support when choosing an upstream service for anything important.
Worked Example

Imagine an MCP server that calls a payments API using a single long lived key stored as an environment variable. The team learns the key may have been exposed in a shared debugging session, and needs to rotate it without taking the server down.
The payments provider supports issuing a second active key before revoking the first, so the team generates a new key in the provider's dashboard while the old one stays valid.

Once monitoring shows the server is successfully using the new key for every recent call, the team revokes the old key in the provider's dashboard. The whole rotation happens without a single restart or a moment of downtime.
The team also updates their incident notes with exactly when the old key was revoked, so anyone reviewing the leak later has a clear timeline.
Common Mistakes
Most secret leaks trace back to one of a small handful of habits, all of them easy to avoid once you know to look for them.

items: Typing a real API key or password directly into a source file, even temporarily, for a quick test
Committing a local environment file that was never added to the ignore list
Logging full request objects or config dumps that happen to include a credential field
Giving a secret far broader access than the task it supports actually needs
Revoking an old secret before confirming the new one is actually working
Caching a secret in memory forever instead of refreshing it, which means rotation silently does nothing until a restart

blocks.text: Practice

Take a small MCP server, real or a practice one you build for this exercise, and find every place a credential is used. Move any hardcoded value out into an environment variable, add a startup check that fails loudly if it is missing, and add a short ignore list entry for any local environment file.
Then simulate a rotation, generate a second dummy value, swap it in through your loading mechanism, and confirm the server picks it up without a restart before you remove the old one.
Key Takeaway

An MCP server almost always holds real secrets, upstream API keys, database credentials, and OAuth client secrets among them, and every one of those must stay out of source code entirely. Environment variables and dedicated secret stores exist precisely so a credential can change without anyone editing a file.
Design the server to fetch its secrets rather than freeze them at startup, and rotation becomes a routine, low risk operation instead of a stressful emergency.
